summary: At nearly 45 square miles, Chino Hills sprawls across more land than the city of San Francisco — yet houses fewer than 78,000 people, which explains why the terrain itself dominates daily life here more than any building does. The city sits on the western edge of the Inland Empire, draped across the Puente Hills and Chino Hills ridgelines, meaning many residential streets tilt at grades steep enough to double as leg workouts, and west-facing homes often catch wide sunset views over the San Gabriel Valley toward distant L.A. basin skyline. That geography also delivers direct access to Chino Hills State Park, a 14,000-acre expanse of grassland and oak woodland threaded with over 60 miles of trails — a genuinely unusual backyard for a suburb of this size. The tradeoff is classic bedroom-community math: a median home price of $830,000 against a median household income of $122,600 yields a price-to-income ratio near 6.8×, which keeps homeownership out of comfortable reach for many at the median. Commuting reinforces the pattern — the city sits between the 71 and 60 freeways, feeding workers toward Orange County, downtown L.A., and Ontario, but hosting relatively few large employers of its own. With 9.5 hours of daily sunshine on average, 77°F daytime highs, and a violent crime rate of just 77.5 per 100,000, the environment is calm and sun-drenched, though retail and dining cluster in strip-mall corridors along Grand Avenue and Peyton Drive rather than any walkable downtown core. Chino Hills is essentially a landscape with a suburb attached — the hills and open space are the draw, and the car commute is the price of admission.
